script.opening: (Genial, dismissive about the ear, keen to talk about his knee.) "I'm really here about my knee, doc, but the wife told me to show you this thing on my ear while I'm on. It's just a scab that won't heal — I keep catching it with my glasses and knocking it, so it never gets the chance. It'll sort itself out eventually, won't it? Don't make a fuss over it."

facts.text: Upper rim of the right ear. "About four months. It bleeds if I knock it, scabs over, looks like it's going, then it breaks down again. It's never actually healed." "It's got a bit bigger, I'd say. It's tender if I press it." About the size of a fingernail now. Will turn his head to the camera; his wife can hold the phone close or send a photo.
If asked about lumps in front of or behind the ear or in the neck: "Not that I've noticed."

"Forty-odd years on golf courses. Never wore a hat much. Fair skin — I always burnt. I had a spot frozen off my head a while back." Rough, scaly patches on his bald scalp and backs of hands. No sunbeds.
Amlodipine 5 mg for blood pressure, paracetamol for the knee. No immunosuppressants, no transplant. No allergies.

Right knee: aching for a year, worse on stairs and after walking the dog, stiff for 10 minutes in the morning, no locking or giving way, no swelling or redness. Wants "something stronger than paracetamol".
Retired greenkeeper, lives with wife, Margaret. Ex-smoker. A couple of pints at the club on Sundays. Plays bowls.

Cheerful and dismissive about the ear. If the doctor pursues it: "If you must. Go on then." If asked what his wife thinks: "She keeps going on that it's been too long. I suppose… I've wondered. But I didn't want to be told something I don't want to hear." Prefers it straight: "Straight. I'd rather know." At the word cancer: "Cancer? From a scab?" Then practical: "What happens next, then?" If the doctor only deals with the knee, go along happily (the trap).

ice.ideas: "It's a scab I keep knocking with my glasses."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he has wondered for a while why it won't heal, and his wife is worried; he hasn't wanted to hear bad news.
ice.expectations: "Sort my knee out, and tell me the ear's nothing."

cues: "The wife told me to show you." — someone else is worried.
"It's never actually healed." — the key red flag, if asked.
"I suppose… I've wondered." — his own worry, if explored.

checkpoints.text: Recognises a NON-HEALING, enlarging, crusting/bleeding lesion on a sun-exposed site in an older sun-damaged person as a likely keratinocyte skin cancer — not accepting the "just a scab I keep knocking" explanation

Differentiates the likely SCC (rapid growth, tender, scaly/crusted, non-healing ulcer/nodule — can metastasise) from BCC (pearly, telangiectasia, rolled edge, slow), and keeps keratoacanthoma/amelanotic melanoma in mind
Takes the SUN-DAMAGE/OCCUPATIONAL history (outdoor work, fair skin, cumulative UV, prior skin cancers, surrounding actinic keratoses/solar elastosis) recognising it raises pre-test probability

EXAMINES and documents the lesion (site, size, morphology) AND the draining regional nodes (pre-/post-auricular, parotid, cervical) given metastatic potential of ear SCC — recognising that a video call shows the lesion but cannot replace palpation, so arranging a prompt face-to-face examination

Applies NICE NG12: considers a suspected cancer pathway referral for a lesion suggesting SCC (and uses the suspected cancer pathway for suspected melanoma); knows BCC is usually routine, suspected cancer pathway only if delay could matter because of site or size — and refers this lesion on the suspected cancer pathway

Takes the incidental "just a scab" mention seriously, gently corrects the "it’ll heal itself" belief, and is honest about needing specialist assessment without alarming him into disengagement — while acknowledging the knee he came for
Explains the referral and reasoning clearly and checks understanding, balancing honesty with reassurance (many are treatable, especially caught early)

Safety-nets and follows up: makes the suspected cancer pathway referral promptly, gives sun-protection and actinic-keratosis advice, advises what change warrants sooner review (rapid growth, bleeding, new lesions/nodes), addresses the knee, confirms attendance, and reviews the outcome — urgent referral, not "leave it to heal"

worked.txt: "I’m glad your wife sent you in with it — we’ll definitely sort your knee, but let me have a proper look at that ear on the camera first, because something that won’t heal for months is worth taking seriously, not brushing off."

"I know it feels like just a scab you keep knocking — but here’s the thing: ordinary skin heals even if you catch it now and then. A spot that keeps breaking down and growing over months is behaving differently, and that’s what I want a specialist to check."

"You were a greenkeeper — years outdoors, fair skin, and you’ve had a spot frozen off before. That all matters. Could you turn so I can see it on the camera? … There’s sun damage around it too. I can’t feel the glands around your ear and neck over video, so I’d like you in to the surgery today or tomorrow so I can examine it and them properly."

"I want to be straight with you. This has the features of a skin cancer — most likely the type called a squamous cell, which we don’t leave to heal. I’m referring you on the suspected cancer pathway to the skin specialists, which means you’re seen quickly and should have an answer within about four weeks. The good news is these are very treatable, especially caught now."
"Going forward, hat and high-factor sun cream on your ears, scalp and face — the damage is cumulative. Now — let’s also properly sort that knee you came in about; I haven’t forgotten it."

"If it grows quickly, bleeds a lot, or you notice new lumps near it before the appointment, contact us sooner. I’ll get the referral done today and we’ll go through whatever they find together. You did the right thing showing me."

f.learning: A lesion that does NOT HEAL over weeks to months — enlarging, crusting, bleeding and repeatedly breaking down — on a sun-exposed site in an older, sun-damaged person is a keratinocyte skin cancer until proven otherwise, and "I keep knocking it, so it won’t heal" is the classic explanation that masks malignancy: normal skin and benign knocks heal, a persistently non-healing lesion does not. Differentiate SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA (rapidly growing, often tender, scaly/crusted/keratotic nodule or non-healing ulcer on ear/face/scalp/lip/hands, with metastatic potential — especially ear and lip) from BASAL CELL CARCINOMA (slow, pearly, telangiectatic, rolled edge, central ulceration, rarely metastasises), keeping keratoacanthoma and amelanotic melanoma in mind; rapid growth, tenderness and breakdown favour SCC. Take the sun-damage/occupational history (outdoor work, fair skin, cumulative UV, prior skin cancers, surrounding actinic keratoses/solar elastosis), which raises pre-test probability, and look at the lesion on camera, then arrange a face-to-face examination documenting the lesion AND the draining regional nodes (pre-/post-auricular, parotid, cervical) given the metastatic risk of ear SCC. NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026): consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for a lesion suggesting SCC (suspected melanoma is also referred on the suspected cancer pathway); BCC is usually a routine referral, suspected cancer pathway only where delay could have a significant impact because of site or size — so this SCC-favouring lesion on a high-risk site (ear, BAD 2020) goes on the suspected cancer pathway. Nodes cannot be palpated on video, so arrange a prompt face-to-face examination. Do not be deflected by the incidental "just a scab" framing in a patient who came about something else: take the mention seriously, gently correct the "it’ll heal itself" belief, refer on the suspected cancer pathway, give sun-protection/actinic-keratosis advice (BAD actinic keratosis guideline 2017), address the original complaint too, and safety-net — never "leave it to heal".

knowledge.guideline: BAD guidelines for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (2020) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BAD guidelines for actinic keratosis (2017)
knowledge.summary: A crusted, enlarging, tender lump on the ear that has not healed for four months, in a fair-skinned lifelong outdoor worker, is a keratinocyte cancer until proven otherwise. The features favour squamous cell carcinoma, which is referred on the suspected cancer pathway.

points.t: Ordinary grazes heal within weeks even if knocked now and then. A lesion that crusts, bleeds, partly heals and breaks down again over months on sun-exposed skin needs a specialist diagnosis, whatever the patient’s explanation.

Squamous cell carcinoma tends to grow over weeks to months and is often tender, keratotic or crusted, or an ulcer. Basal cell carcinoma is usually slow, pearly, with a rolled edge and fine vessels, and may ulcerate centrally. Keratoacanthoma and amelanotic melanoma are in the differential; neither is safe to watch.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral (appointment within 2 weeks) for a skin lesion that raises the suspicion of squamous cell carcinoma. For a suspected basal cell carcinoma, consider routine referral, and use the suspected cancer pathway only if there is particular concern that a delay could have a significant impact because of factors such as site or size.

BAD 2020 treats the ear and lip as high-risk sites for cutaneous SCC. Examine and record the lesion (site, size, appearance) and feel the draining nodes: pre- and post-auricular, parotid and neck. A video call can show the lesion but cannot replace palpation, so arrange a face-to-face examination promptly.

Actinic keratoses and sun-damaged skin around the lesion mark cumulative UV damage and raise the chance of further skin cancers. BAD 2017: treat or monitor actinic keratoses, advise sun protection, and check the rest of the sun-exposed skin.

Hat with a brim, high-factor broad-spectrum sunscreen on the ears, scalp and face, and shade in the middle of the day. Anyone with one keratinocyte cancer is at risk of more: teach self-checks of the scalp, ears and hands.

dg.d: Gathered the full agenda at the start; negotiated looking at the ear first without dismissing the knee.
Lifelong outdoor work, sun habits, his wife’s concern, his wish to avoid a fuss, and how he likes information given.
Inspected via the camera; arranged face-to-face palpation of the pre/post-auricular, parotid and cervical nodes; photo for the referral.
SCC vs BCC vs keratoacanthoma vs amelanotic melanoma; used growth, tenderness and crusting to weigh them.
Asked about nodes and other non-healing lesions; knew ear SCC can spread; did not accept watch-and-wait.
Likely cutaneous SCC on a high-risk site, stated plainly with realistic hope.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Suspected cancer pathway referral today (NICE NG12); wound care; glasses adjustment; sun protection.
Actinic keratoses and field change (BAD 2017); the knee dealt with at the same face-to-face visit.
Named changes that warrant sooner contact; told him to chase the appointment if not heard within a week; teach-back; continuity.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “it won’t heal” and “the wife told me” as cues, and his quiet worry behind the minimisation.
Idea (a scab he keeps knocking); concern (being told bad news, a fuss); expectation (reassurance, focus on the knee).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Frost, I’m Dr Lee. Can you see and hear me all right? … Good. I know you’ve booked about your knee, and we will deal with it. You mentioned your wife wanted me to see your ear too — can you tell me about both, so we can plan the time?
model.why: Checks the video link and gathers the whole agenda at the start

model.text: The knee’s the main thing, doc. The ear’s just a scab that won’t heal — I keep catching it with my glasses so it never gets a chance. It’ll sort itself out, won’t it? Don’t make a fuss.
I hear you — you don’t want a fuss. Can I spend a couple of minutes on the ear first, then give the knee proper attention? Something that hasn’t healed for a while is worth a careful look.
model.why: Respects his wish while negotiating the order of the agenda

model.text: If you must. Go on then.
How long has it been there, and what has it been doing?
model.why: Opens the history of the lesion

model.text: About four months. It bleeds if I knock it, scabs over, looks like it’s going, then it breaks down again. It’s never actually healed.
Has it changed in size, and is it sore?
model.why: Asks about growth and tenderness, which point towards SCC

model.text: It’s got a bit bigger, I’d say. It’s tender if I press it.
Could you tilt the camera so I can see it, as close as the picture will focus? … Thank you. I can see a crusted, raised lump on the rim of your right ear, and rough, sun-damaged skin around it.
model.why: Uses the video to inspect and describes the lesion

model.text: That’s the one. Looks worse on the screen, doesn’t it?
Tell me about the sun over the years. You were a greenkeeper — outdoors most days?
model.why: Takes the occupational and UV history

model.text: Forty-odd years on golf courses. Never wore a hat much. Fair skin — I always burnt. I had a spot frozen off my head a while back.
That’s really useful. Have you noticed any lumps near your ear or in your neck, or any other sores that won’t heal?
model.why: Screens for nodal spread and other lesions

model.text: Not that I’ve noticed.
You said your wife sent you in with it. What does she think — and, honestly, what have you been thinking?
model.why: Follows the cue that someone else is worried and explores his own view

model.text: She keeps going on that it’s been too long. I suppose… I’ve wondered. But I didn’t want to be told something I don’t want to hear.
Thank you for being honest. That’s a very human reaction. What would you want from me today — the straight version, or the gentle version?
model.why: Validates avoidance and asks how he wants information

model.text: Straight. I’d rather know.

Then here it is straight. Ordinary skin heals, even if you knock it now and then. A spot that keeps breaking down and growing over four months, on sun-damaged skin, is behaving like a skin cancer. The most likely type is called a squamous cell carcinoma.
model.why: Names the working diagnosis honestly and explains why

model.text: Cancer? From a scab?

It can look just like a scab — that’s why it’s easy to miss. The good news is these are usually very treatable, especially when they’re dealt with early, and the usual treatment is a small operation to remove it. But this is one to act on now, not to leave to heal.
What happens next, then?

I’m going to refer you today on the urgent suspected cancer pathway to the skin team, so you’re seen within two weeks. I also want to see you in person this week, to feel the glands around your ear and neck — I can’t do that over video — and to look at your knee properly at the same visit.
model.why: Suspected cancer pathway referral per NICE NG12, plus face-to-face node examination

model.text: Two birds with one stone. That suits me.
Could you take a clear photo of the ear and send it to the surgery? It helps the specialists. Until then, keep it clean and covered, and try moving your glasses arm or padding it so it isn’t rubbed.
model.why: Practical steps that support the referral and wound care

model.text: My wife can do the photo. She’ll be glad.

She’ll be glad you listened to her. One more thing for the future: your skin has had a lot of sun, so the risk of more of these is higher. A hat with a brim and high-factor sun cream on your ears, scalp and face, even on cloudy days, and have a look at your scalp and hands every month or so.
model.why: Prevention and self-surveillance tailored to him

model.text: Right. The wife will make sure of that too.

If it suddenly grows, bleeds heavily, or you notice a new lump by your ear or in your neck before the appointment, ring us straight away. And if you haven’t heard about the appointment within a week, ring us so we can chase it.
model.why: Specific safety-net and ownership of the referral

model.text: Will do.
To check I’ve explained it well, what will you tell your wife tonight?

That she was right. It might be a skin cancer, probably the treatable sort, and I’m being seen urgently in two weeks. I’m coming in this week for you to feel my neck and look at my knee. Hat and sun cream.
Spot on. You did the right thing showing me. I’ll see you this week — and we’ll go through whatever the skin team finds together. Anything else before we finish?
No — thanks, doc. Better to know.

social.t: Decades of outdoor work with little sun protection is the key risk. Many outdoor workers underplay skin changes; his wife’s push is an asset — involve her with his permission.
“Don’t make a fuss” often hides fear of bad news. Asking how he wants information given lets him hear it.

legal.t: Get his consent before a photo of the lesion goes into the record or with the referral, and store it securely in the clinical system.

professional.t: Good practice is to track suspected cancer referrals and tell the patient to chase if he hears nothing. Document the lesion description, the NICE NG12 basis and the advice given (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Recognise what cannot be done remotely — palpating nodes — and arrange face-to-face examination rather than relying on the screen alone.

community.t: British Association of Dermatologists patient information on squamous cell carcinoma, actinic keratoses and sun protection; the NHS sun-safety advice pages.

redFlags: Non-healing for weeks to months, enlarging, bleeding or tender lesion on sun-exposed skin
New lumps near the ear or in the neck (possible nodal spread)
Pigmented or changing lesion — think melanoma
psychosocial: Lifelong outdoor work and sun habits; fair skin; previous treated lesion
His wife’s concern and his wish to avoid a fuss
Practical issues: glasses rubbing the ear, getting to appointments, the knee
ice: Idea: “Just a scab I keep knocking with my glasses”
Concern: being told something he doesn’t want to hear; making a fuss
Expectation: reassurance about the ear and attention to his knee

playbook.diagnosis: A crusted, enlarging, tender lesion that has not healed for four months on the helix of a sun-damaged man is most likely a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma; BCC, keratoacanthoma and amelanotic melanoma are the main alternatives. The ear is a high-risk site, so examine the nodes and refer on the suspected cancer pathway.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Normal skin heals even if you knock it. This spot keeps breaking down and growing, which is how a common type of skin cancer behaves. It’s usually very treatable, often with a small operation, but it needs a specialist to see it soon rather than waiting for it to heal.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought it was just a scab you keep catching with your glasses — and I understand why. But your wife was right to send you in, and you were right to show me.”
management.psychosocial: Give the news the way he asked — straight — with realistic hope. Combine the node check and the knee in one visit so the practical burden is low, and involve his wife if he wishes.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral today for suspected SCC (NICE NG12) with a photo, with consent
Face-to-face this week: lesion, regional nodes, other sun-exposed skin, and the knee
Keep the lesion clean and covered, stop the glasses rubbing it; hat and high-factor sunscreen; actinic keratosis care (BAD 2017)
safetyNet: Rapid growth, heavy bleeding or a new lump near the ear or in the neck — contact the surgery straight away
No appointment letter within a week — ring the surgery to chase; review the outcome together

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed when the candidate is steered by the patient’s framing — a scab, a knee — and never treats the ear as a possible cancer. The patterns below are drawn from recurring SCA feedback.

items.fail: Accepting “I keep knocking it” and advising him to leave it to heal, or prescribing an antibiotic or steroid cream.
items.why: “Management not in line with current UK best practice.” A four-month non-healing lesion on sun-damaged skin needs referral, not treatment trials.
items.fix: “Normal skin heals even if you catch it. This hasn’t in four months, so I want a specialist to see it.”

items.fail: Labelling it a BCC and making a routine referral.
items.why: Growth, tenderness and crusting on the ear favour SCC; NICE NG12 supports a suspected cancer pathway referral for suspected SCC.
items.fix: Say the discriminating features aloud, then refer on the suspected cancer pathway.

items.fail: Never considering the nodes, or claiming to have examined them over video.
items.why: “Did not gather sufficient information to make a safe diagnosis.” Ear SCC can spread to regional nodes, and palpation needs a face-to-face visit.
items.fix: Ask about lumps now and book an in-person examination this week.

items.fail: Dropping the knee entirely, or rushing the ear to get back to the knee.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s agenda.” He came about the knee; ignoring it loses his trust.
items.fix: Agree the order at the start, and fold the knee into the face-to-face visit.

items.fail: Blurting “this is cancer” to a man who has spent months avoiding the thought — or hiding the word altogether.
items.why: Both extremes fail: shock causes disengagement, vagueness leaves him unprepared.
items.fix: Ask how he wants the news, then name it honestly with realistic hope: “usually very treatable, especially dealt with early.”

items.fail: Closing with “the hospital will be in touch” and no safety-net.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no ownership of the referral are standard failing statements.
items.fix: Name what would warrant sooner contact, tell him to chase if nothing arrives within a week, and use teach-back.

timeMap.d: Get both problems on the table. Agree to look at the ear first and promise the knee its time.
Duration, growth, bleeding, tenderness, never healed. Ask him to angle the camera. Sun and occupational history, previous frozen lesion, lumps in the neck.
Why did his wife send him? What has he been thinking? Ask how he wants the news — straight or gentle.
Name likely SCC honestly with realistic hope. Suspected cancer pathway today. Face-to-face this week for nodes and the knee. Photo, wound care, sun protection.
What would warrant sooner contact; chase if no appointment within a week; teach-back; continuity.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “just a scab” and advises leaving it to heal or a cream; or ignores the ear to finish the knee; no sun history; no plan to examine nodes; no referral or a routine one; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Takes the ear seriously, gathers the lesion and sun history, recognises likely SCC, makes a suspected cancer pathway referral, arranges node examination and gives basic sun advice and a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: negotiates the agenda without losing the knee; draws out his quiet worry and asks how he wants news; names the diagnosis honestly with realistic hope; combines the node check and knee in one face-to-face visit; teach-back and ownership of the referral.

avoid.dont: "It’s probably just a scab — keep it covered and see how it goes."
avoid.instead: "Ordinary skin heals. A spot that keeps breaking down for four months needs a specialist look."
avoid.why: Watch-and-wait on a likely SCC is unsafe management.

avoid.dont: "It looks like a BCC, those are slow, so I’ll send a routine referral."
avoid.instead: "Because it’s on your ear, it’s growing and it’s tender, I’m referring you urgently."
avoid.why: Growth, tenderness and crusting on the ear favour SCC, which NICE NG12 refers on the suspected cancer pathway.

avoid.dont: "We’ll deal with the ear another time — let’s do your knee."
avoid.instead: "Can I spend a couple of minutes on the ear first, then give your knee proper attention?"
avoid.why: The incidental problem is the dangerous one; it must be addressed without dropping his own agenda.

It can look just like a scab — that’s why it’s easy to miss. The good news is these are usually very treatable, especially when they’re dealt with early, and the usual treatment is a small operation to remove it. But this is one to act on now, not to leave to heal.
What happens next, then?

I’m going to refer you today on the urgent suspected cancer pathway to the skin team, so you’re seen within two weeks. I also want to see you in person this week, to feel the glands around your ear and neck — I can’t do that over video — and to look at your knee properly at the same visit.
SCA_MODELS.why: Suspected cancer pathway referral per NICE NG12, plus face-to-face node examination

SCA_MODELS.text: Two birds with one stone. That suits me.
Could you take a clear photo of the ear and send it to the surgery? It helps the specialists. Until then, keep it clean and covered, and try moving your glasses arm or padding it so it isn’t rubbed.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical steps that support the referral and wound care

SCA_MODELS.text: My wife can do the photo. She’ll be glad.

She’ll be glad you listened to her. One more thing for the future: your skin has had a lot of sun, so the risk of more of these is higher. A hat with a brim and high-factor sun cream on your ears, scalp and face, even on cloudy days, and have a look at your scalp and hands every month or so.
SCA_MODELS.why: Prevention and self-surveillance tailored to him

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. The wife will make sure of that too.

If it suddenly grows, bleeds heavily, or you notice a new lump by your ear or in your neck before the appointment, ring us straight away. And if you haven’t heard about the appointment within a week, ring us so we can chase it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net and ownership of the referral

SCA_MODELS.text: Will do.
To check I’ve explained it well, what will you tell your wife tonight?

That she was right. It might be a skin cancer, probably the treatable sort, and I’m being seen urgently in two weeks. I’m coming in this week for you to feel my neck and look at my knee. Hat and sun cream.
Spot on. You did the right thing showing me. I’ll see you this week — and we’ll go through whatever the skin team finds together. Anything else before we finish?
No — thanks, doc. Better to know.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BAD guidelines for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (2020) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BAD guidelines for actinic keratosis (2017)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A crusted, enlarging, tender lump on the ear that has not healed for four months, in a fair-skinned lifelong outdoor worker, is a keratinocyte cancer until proven otherwise. The features favour squamous cell carcinoma, which is referred on the suspected cancer pathway.

points.t: Ordinary grazes heal within weeks even if knocked now and then. A lesion that crusts, bleeds, partly heals and breaks down again over months on sun-exposed skin needs a specialist diagnosis, whatever the patient’s explanation.

Squamous cell carcinoma tends to grow over weeks to months and is often tender, keratotic or crusted, or an ulcer. Basal cell carcinoma is usually slow, pearly, with a rolled edge and fine vessels, and may ulcerate centrally. Keratoacanthoma and amelanotic melanoma are in the differential; neither is safe to watch.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral (appointment within 2 weeks) for a skin lesion that raises the suspicion of squamous cell carcinoma. For a suspected basal cell carcinoma, consider routine referral, and use the suspected cancer pathway only if there is particular concern that a delay could have a significant impact because of factors such as site or size.

BAD 2020 treats the ear and lip as high-risk sites for cutaneous SCC. Examine and record the lesion (site, size, appearance) and feel the draining nodes: pre- and post-auricular, parotid and neck. A video call can show the lesion but cannot replace palpation, so arrange a face-to-face examination promptly.

Actinic keratoses and sun-damaged skin around the lesion mark cumulative UV damage and raise the chance of further skin cancers. BAD 2017: treat or monitor actinic keratoses, advise sun protection, and check the rest of the sun-exposed skin.

Hat with a brim, high-factor broad-spectrum sunscreen on the ears, scalp and face, and shade in the middle of the day. Anyone with one keratinocyte cancer is at risk of more: teach self-checks of the scalp, ears and hands.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Gathered the full agenda at the start; negotiated looking at the ear first without dismissing the knee.
Lifelong outdoor work, sun habits, his wife’s concern, his wish to avoid a fuss, and how he likes information given.
Picked up “it won’t heal” and “the wife told me” as cues, and his quiet worry behind the minimisation.
Idea (a scab he keeps knocking); concern (being told bad news, a fuss); expectation (reassurance, focus on the knee).
Inspected via the camera; arranged face-to-face palpation of the pre/post-auricular, parotid and cervical nodes; photo for the referral.
SCC vs BCC vs keratoacanthoma vs amelanotic melanoma; used growth, tenderness and crusting to weigh them.
Asked about nodes and other non-healing lesions; knew ear SCC can spread; did not accept watch-and-wait.
Likely cutaneous SCC on a high-risk site, stated plainly with realistic hope.
Suspected cancer pathway referral today (NICE NG12); wound care; glasses adjustment; sun protection.
Actinic keratoses and field change (BAD 2017); the knee dealt with at the same face-to-face visit.
Named changes that warrant sooner contact; told him to chase the appointment if not heard within a week; teach-back; continuity.

social.t: Decades of outdoor work with little sun protection is the key risk. Many outdoor workers underplay skin changes; his wife’s push is an asset — involve her with his permission.
“Don’t make a fuss” often hides fear of bad news. Asking how he wants information given lets him hear it.

legal.t: Get his consent before a photo of the lesion goes into the record or with the referral, and store it securely in the clinical system.

professional.t: Good practice is to track suspected cancer referrals and tell the patient to chase if he hears nothing. Document the lesion description, the NICE NG12 basis and the advice given (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Recognise what cannot be done remotely — palpating nodes — and arrange face-to-face examination rather than relying on the screen alone.

community.t: British Association of Dermatologists patient information on squamous cell carcinoma, actinic keratoses and sun protection; the NHS sun-safety advice pages.

redFlags: Non-healing for weeks to months, enlarging, bleeding or tender lesion on sun-exposed skin
New lumps near the ear or in the neck (possible nodal spread)
Pigmented or changing lesion — think melanoma
psychosocial: Lifelong outdoor work and sun habits; fair skin; previous treated lesion
His wife’s concern and his wish to avoid a fuss
Practical issues: glasses rubbing the ear, getting to appointments, the knee
ice: Idea: “Just a scab I keep knocking with my glasses”
Concern: being told something he doesn’t want to hear; making a fuss
Expectation: reassurance about the ear and attention to his knee

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: A crusted, enlarging, tender lesion that has not healed for four months on the helix of a sun-damaged man is most likely a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma; BCC, keratoacanthoma and amelanotic melanoma are the main alternatives. The ear is a high-risk site, so examine the nodes and refer on the suspected cancer pathway.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Normal skin heals even if you knock it. This spot keeps breaking down and growing, which is how a common type of skin cancer behaves. It’s usually very treatable, often with a small operation, but it needs a specialist to see it soon rather than waiting for it to heal.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought it was just a scab you keep catching with your glasses — and I understand why. But your wife was right to send you in, and you were right to show me.”
management.psychosocial: Give the news the way he asked — straight — with realistic hope. Combine the node check and the knee in one visit so the practical burden is low, and involve his wife if he wishes.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral today for suspected SCC (NICE NG12) with a photo, with consent
Face-to-face this week: lesion, regional nodes, other sun-exposed skin, and the knee
Keep the lesion clean and covered, stop the glasses rubbing it; hat and high-factor sunscreen; actinic keratosis care (BAD 2017)
safetyNet: Rapid growth, heavy bleeding or a new lump near the ear or in the neck — contact the surgery straight away
No appointment letter within a week — ring the surgery to chase; review the outcome together

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed when the candidate is steered by the patient’s framing — a scab, a knee — and never treats the ear as a possible cancer. The patterns below are drawn from recurring SCA feedback.

items.fail: Accepting “I keep knocking it” and advising him to leave it to heal, or prescribing an antibiotic or steroid cream.
items.why: “Management not in line with current UK best practice.” A four-month non-healing lesion on sun-damaged skin needs referral, not treatment trials.
items.fix: “Normal skin heals even if you catch it. This hasn’t in four months, so I want a specialist to see it.”

items.fail: Labelling it a BCC and making a routine referral.
items.why: Growth, tenderness and crusting on the ear favour SCC; NICE NG12 supports a suspected cancer pathway referral for suspected SCC.
items.fix: Say the discriminating features aloud, then refer on the suspected cancer pathway.

items.fail: Never considering the nodes, or claiming to have examined them over video.
items.why: “Did not gather sufficient information to make a safe diagnosis.” Ear SCC can spread to regional nodes, and palpation needs a face-to-face visit.
items.fix: Ask about lumps now and book an in-person examination this week.

items.fail: Dropping the knee entirely, or rushing the ear to get back to the knee.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s agenda.” He came about the knee; ignoring it loses his trust.
items.fix: Agree the order at the start, and fold the knee into the face-to-face visit.

items.fail: Blurting “this is cancer” to a man who has spent months avoiding the thought — or hiding the word altogether.
items.why: Both extremes fail: shock causes disengagement, vagueness leaves him unprepared.
items.fix: Ask how he wants the news, then name it honestly with realistic hope: “usually very treatable, especially dealt with early.”

items.fail: Closing with “the hospital will be in touch” and no safety-net.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no ownership of the referral are standard failing statements.
items.fix: Name what would warrant sooner contact, tell him to chase if nothing arrives within a week, and use teach-back.
